stories.title: A school tax with a different tax base
stories.dek: On November 3, district voters decide a five-year, 1% earned income tax. Retirement income would be excluded.
stories.body:
The proposed tax would apply to qualifying wages, salaries, tips and self-employment income. Retirement income, interest, dividends, capital gains and unemployment benefits would be excluded.

The district has already cut or left unfilled 25 teaching positions, one administrator and numerous support positions for 2026–27. It also canceled three planned bus purchases—not three bus routes.

Even with those reductions, its August General Fund forecast projects cash reserves running out in fiscal 2029 without further changes. That is a forecast of trouble ahead, not a statement that the checking account is empty today.

stories.title: An assisted-living proposal on College Street
stories.dek: The plan: three stories, 120 units and 6.5 acres at 823 College St. The zoning still needs Council approval.
stories.body:
The proposed assisted-living facility cleared a step September 28: Planning Commission recommended changing the property to R-2 residential zoning, The Gazette’s Brooke Adams reported.

Council is scheduled to discuss the draft October 6. That is a zoning decision, not a green light for the building.

One detail matters beyond this proposal: the new zoning would stay even if the facility never gets built. A tentative November 17 public hearing has been reported, but the date is not final.

stories.title: A better shelter for dogs between homes
stories.dek: Medina County’s roughly $6 million replacement plan includes indoor play areas, adoption space and on-site veterinary care.
stories.body:
The existing dog shelter dates to 1974, and county officials say it has outlived its useful life. The planned replacement would add better ventilation, daylight and room for dogs to meet prospective adopters.

Commissioners authorized a donation fund September 22 to help pay for construction and related debt.

The projected schedule calls for bidding in late 2026, groundbreaking by early 2027 and opening in early 2028. Those are targets, not appointments you should put the dog in the car for yet.

stories.dek: First-edition catch-up: Officials confirmed access July 13, with hoops installed that day.

stories.title: County proposes four-permit limit to press fiber companies on restoration
stories.dek: September catch-up: The proposed process also calls for advance resident notice; legal review remained pending.
stories.body:
Medina County Engineer Andy Conrad proposed limiting each fiber company to four open county permits at a time on September 8, 2026. Companies would have to finish work, pass inspections and verify restoration before receiving additional permits.

Conrad described the proposal as a response to long gaps between conduit installation and fiber deployment that left residents’ yards disrupted for months. He also proposed advance notice to residents, plans for the affected township, and notices when work starts and finishes so inspectors can follow up.

The proposal concerns the county’s permit process. Conrad said rollout depended on review by the Prosecutor’s Office; the September discussion did not establish that the requirements had taken effect.

editorial.residentValue: Explains proposed notice and restoration protections for residents affected by county-permitted fiber work, with adoption status clearly limited.
editorial.change: The county engineer proposed a four-open-permit cap and additional notice and inspection requirements.
editorial.whyNow: First-edition catch-up explains a consequential September proposal addressing prolonged property disruption; it is not presented as an enacted rule.

evidenceRefs.assertion: The discussion occurred September 8, 2026.
evidenceRefs.quote: TUESDAY, SEPTEMBER 8, 2026

evidenceRefs.assertion: County Engineer Andy Conrad proposed administrative changes for fiber installation oversight.
evidenceRefs.quote:
County Engineer Andy Conrad led a discussion on a proposed set of administrative process changes intended to
improve oversight of fiber installation companies operating within the county.

evidenceRefs.assertion: Proposed requirements include advance resident notification, township plans, a four-open-permit limit, restoration verification and start/completion notices; Conrad described months-long yard disruption.
evidenceRefs.quote:
Mr. Conrad outlined several proposed changes. First, he proposed requiring fiber companies to provide advance
notifications to residents and to furnish a set of plans to the township in which they are working, as townships
frequently report having no knowledge of ongoing installations. Second, and most significantly, he proposed
limiting each fiber company to a maximum of four open permits at one time. This would compel companies to
complete and close out permitted work — including final inspections and restoration verification — before being
issued additional permits. Currently, companies pull large numbers of permits simultaneously, and significant delays
occur between conduit installation and actual fiber deployment, leaving residents’ yards disrupted for months at a
time. Third, he proposed requiring companies to provide advance notice when work is beginning so the Engineer’s
Office can conduct inspections, and to notify the office upon completion so a closing inspection can be performed
before the permit is officially closed.

evidenceRefs.assertion: The discussion concerns county road permitting and distinguishes it from more limited oversight of private utility easements.
evidenceRefs.quote:
Discussion touched on the distinction between the public road right-of-way — where the county has clear bonding
and permitting authority — and private utility easements, where oversight is more limited

evidenceRefs.assertion: Rollout was contingent on prosecutor review and was not reported as completed.
evidenceRefs.quote:
Mr. Conrad indicated that, pending a review by the Prosecutor’s Office, he intends to roll out the new process to the
fiber companies.

stories.dek: September catch-up: The county aggregation terms run through April 2029 and differ by utility.

Medina County commissioners authorized new fixed gas-supply terms September 1 for the county aggregation program: $6.849 per MCF for Columbia Gas customers and $4.959 per MCF for Enbridge customers. The listed term covers October 2026 through April 2029 meter reads.

The opt-out program covers eligible residents and businesses in unincorporated county areas. The authorization does not establish that City of Wadsworth customers participate.

The new Archer Energy terms would replace a variable-rate agreement that extended through the March 2027 meter read. Commissioners authorized the county administrator to execute the necessary documents. That action establishes the approved terms, but does not confirm contract execution or what an individual customer is being billed.

stories.title: County approves paid election-day leave for eligible poll workers
stories.dek: July catch-up: The November 3 policy requires written approval and covers non-bargaining employees.
stories.body:
Eligible Medina County employees can request paid leave to work the polls November 3 while keeping their regular compensation and receiving poll-worker pay. Commissioners approved the policy July 28 after the Board of Elections reported a staffing shortage for that election.

The policy applies only to non-bargaining employees who meet voter-registration and other election-worker requirements. Employees must obtain written leave authorization before contacting the Board of Elections to register. Other elected county officials may allow their employees to participate under their own terms.

The leave covers election day only, and employees must work the full polling day to receive it. Training during work hours requires separately approved vacation, personal or compensatory leave. Operational needs can prevent approval, and the Board of Elections can decline a placement if the employee is not needed.

editorial.residentValue: Helps eligible employees understand compensation, scheduling and the required approval sequence before committing to election work.
editorial.change: Commissioners approved paid leave for eligible county employees serving as November 3 precinct election officials.
editorial.whyNow: First-edition catch-up concerns an approved opportunity for the November 3 election, 29 days after the cutoff; the July staffing shortage is not presented as a verified October shortage.

    2. All other elected county officials, are authorized, at their sole discretion and under their
       own terms, to permit their employees to obtain paid leave for the purpose of serving as

stories.title: Council requires names and home addresses for public comment
stories.dek: First-edition catch-up: The July 21 rule also sets identification requirements for official written correspondence.
stories.body:
Wadsworth City Council adopted a rule July 21, 2026, requiring speakers to give their full legal name and residential address, including city and state. That information goes into the official meeting record; people who decline cannot speak before Council.

Rule 25 also requires an author’s full legal name and residential address on written submissions intended for the Council record. Submissions lacking that information cannot be read during a meeting, distributed as official correspondence or entered into the official record.

Anonymous complaints can still reach administrators. The clerk may forward matters involving public safety, public health, legal compliance, misuse of public resources or other legitimate public concerns for review. Council is not required to act on them.

The rule permits communications from government agencies, elected officials, public entities, attorneys representing clients and organizations when the submitting individual is clearly identified and contact information is provided.

stories.title: Council authorized two ambulance remounts with a $460,000 ceiling
stories.dek: September catch-up: Officials expected three squads to remain available while the two vehicles were refurbished sequentially.
stories.body:
Wadsworth City Council authorized a contract with Pfund Superior Sales on September 1, 2026, to refurbish two ambulance patient compartments and mount them on new 2027 Ford E-450 cabs and chassis. The spending ceiling is $460,000.

Safety Director Dan Chafin said each vehicle would take approximately 90 days. With the work done sequentially, he expected the department to operate three squads instead of four for about 180 days across the project. That was an anticipated fleet reduction, not confirmation that work had begun.

The quoted price was $226,022 per vehicle. Chafin said the additional authorization would cover possible damage, repairs or vendor price increases. He estimated potential savings of about $100,000 compared with buying two entirely new squads.

The adopted ordinance permits contracting without formal bidding and advertising. It establishes purchasing authority, not completed purchases or delivery.

The proposals would reduce the 1.5-mill fire levy and renew the three-mill EMS levy with an additional mill.

Safety Director Dan Chafin estimated a combined net increase of about $12 a year per $100,000 of the county auditor’s market value once both changes apply. His estimate assumed a state tax rollback on the existing portion of the EMS levy; it is not an individual tax quote.

The city plans to draw down fire reserves as that levy falls. Fire money would not be transferred to EMS. The tax labels may look like a simple swap, but the funding arrangements are separate.

stories.dek: First-edition catch-up: About $6,700 had been recovered through July, with $2,200 in attorney fees accrued.
stories.body:
Wadsworth had referred approximately $991,000 in unpaid utility accounts to Kim & Associates by August 4, 2026, Assistant Service Director Mike Testa reported. The referrals concerned inactive accounts less than six and a half years old with balances above $50; collection efforts included letters and possible legal action.

Through July, approximately $6,700 had been recovered. About $2,200 in attorney fees had accrued but remained unpaid pending an invoice. Testa expected the effort to run approximately two years and cautioned that full recovery was unlikely.

The fee schedule matters: the firm charges 33⅓% on the first $25,000 recovered from each account, with lower rates for larger recoveries. The tiers apply separately to each account, rather than to the entire collection total.

The August 4 report described collection activity already underway. Separately, Council authorized a utility-debt collection contract with the firm on August 18. These dated actions do not establish how much has been recovered since July.

stories.dek: Council is considering a $1.13 million base ceiling for management and inspection—not the construction itself.

The proposal would let Wadsworth hire one or more consulting firms to oversee its Downtown Infrastructure Project. Change orders could add up to 10% of the contract amount.

The proposed “owner’s representative” would work for the city, manage contractor relationships and help oversee construction. Hiscock explained a consequential distinction: unlike a construction manager at risk, that representative would not absorb cost overruns.

Staff hoped to seek construction bids in the fall and award the work during 2026. They also planned to seek authority to interview firms for the representative role. Those were proposed next steps; the August recommendation did not establish a selected firm, a construction award or achieved savings.

projects.location: Wadsworth; individual repair locations not established
projects.description:
Wadsworth’s 2026 sidewalk program planned approximately 3,000 linear feet of repairs with no property assessments, city staff reported July 13. The program budget was $250,000 after budget-season cutbacks.

Council subsequently authorized a contract with T.R. Snyder Construction on August 18, 2026. Public Service Director Matt Hiscock said that day that bids had been received and the contractor was waiting to begin.

The $250,000 figure is the reported program budget, not an established contract price. The no-assessment statement concerns this 2026 program; it does not establish an exemption for other sidewalk work or future years. A completed construction schedule is not established.
